## Where we are

- W02 ended at maximum likelihood in **one** dimension
- Data is not one-dimensional: an MNIST digit is a point in $\mathbb{R}^{784}$
- Today: the one family that survives everything we do to it

::: {.note}
The claim to keep in view: almost every operation in this course is **linear** —
adding noise, blending signal and noise, projecting, marginalising. The Gaussian
is closed under all of them, with parameters you can compute in closed form.
:::

## The density

For $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, with $\Sigma$ symmetric
positive definite,

$$p(x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\,(\det\Sigma)^{1/2}}
\exp\!\Big(-\tfrac12 (x-\mu)^{\!\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\Big)$$

- The exponent is a **quadratic form** — so level sets are ellipsoids, always
- $\mu$ moves the centre; $\Sigma$ sets the shape, spread and tilt
- $\det\Sigma$ in the constant is the volume factor that makes it integrate to 1

## What it costs to go multivariate

A full $\Sigma$ has $\tfrac{d(d+1)}{2}$ free entries, plus $d$ for the mean:

$$\frac{d(d+3)}{2}\ \text{parameters}$$

| $d$ | parameters |
|---|---|
| 2 | 5 |
| 10 | 65 |
| 784 (MNIST) | **308,504** |

::: {.note}
This is the first honest sign of trouble in high dimension — and the reason
structure (diagonal, low-rank, factorised) is not laziness but necessity.
:::

## Identity covariance: the joint *is* a product

Set $\mu = 0$, $\Sigma = I$. The exponent becomes a **sum of squares**, and a sum
in the exponent is a product outside it:

$$p(x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}} e^{-\frac12 \sum_i x_i^2}
= \prod_{i=1}^{d} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x_i^2/2}$$

So $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ is exactly $d$ independent standard normals.

::: {.note}
Diagonal $\Sigma$ $\Rightarrow$ independent coordinates — but **only because it is
Gaussian**. In general, uncorrelated does not imply independent.
:::

## The results, in one table

$X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)$ throughout.

| Result | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Affine map** | $AX + b \sim \mathcal{N}(A\mu + b,\ A\Sigma A^{\!\top})$ |
| **Projection** | $a^{\!\top}X \sim \mathcal{N}(a^{\!\top}\mu,\ a^{\!\top}\Sigma a)$ |
| **Marginal** | $X_S \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_S, \Sigma_{SS})$ — delete the other rows and columns |
| **Independent sum** | $X + Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu+\nu,\ \Sigma + T)$ |
| **Whitening** | $\Sigma = LL^{\!\top} \Rightarrow L^{-1}(X-\mu) \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$ |
| **MGF** | $\mathbb{E}\big[e^{t^{\!\top}X}\big] = \exp\!\big(t^{\!\top}\mu + \tfrac12 t^{\!\top}\Sigma t\big)$ |

The first line is the engine. Everything above it is a special case — and we
prove it now.

## The claim

::: {.note}
**Theorem.** Let $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and let
$A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$. Then

$$Y = AX + b \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\big(A\mu + b,\ A\Sigma A^{\!\top}\big).$$
:::

Two separate things to establish, and it is worth not conflating them:

1. the **mean and covariance** are what the formula says — true for *any*
   distribution with two moments, no normality involved;
2. the result is **still Gaussian** — this is the part with content.

## Step 1 — mean and covariance need no normality

Linearity of expectation:

$$\mathbb{E}[Y] = A\,\mathbb{E}[X] + b = A\mu + b$$

::: {.fragment}
And straight from the definition of covariance, using
$Y - \mathbb{E}[Y] = A(X - \mu)$:

$$\operatorname{Cov}(Y) = \mathbb{E}\big[(Y-\mathbb{E}Y)(Y-\mathbb{E}Y)^{\!\top}\big]
= \mathbb{E}\big[A(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^{\!\top}A^{\!\top}\big]$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$A$ is constant, so it comes outside the expectation:

$$\operatorname{Cov}(Y) = A\,\mathbb{E}\big[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^{\!\top}\big]\,A^{\!\top} = A\Sigma A^{\!\top}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Note $b$ has vanished — shifting cannot change a covariance.
:::

## Detour: the moment generating function

For a random vector $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$,

$$M_X(t) \;=\; \mathbb{E}\big[e^{t^{\!\top}X}\big], \qquad t \in \mathbb{R}^d$$

::: {.fragment}
**Why "moment generating".** Expand $e^{tX} = \sum_k t^k X^k/k!$ and
differentiate at the origin — each derivative pulls down one moment:

$$\nabla M_X(0) = \mu, \qquad \nabla^2 M_X(0) = \mathbb{E}\big[XX^{\!\top}\big] = \Sigma + \mu\mu^{\!\top}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
One function of $t$, carrying every moment of $X$.
:::

## Why the MGF is enough

::: {.note}
**Uniqueness theorem.** If $M_X(t) = M_Y(t)$ for all $t$ in some open
neighbourhood of the origin, then $X$ and $Y$ have the **same distribution**.
:::

The MGF does not merely summarise a law — it *determines* it. That is what
licenses the whole strategy: **compute an MGF, recognise its shape, conclude.**

::: {.fragment}
**The honest caveat.** Not every distribution has an MGF — $\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]$
is infinite for a Cauchy at every $t \ne 0$. The repair is the characteristic
function $\varphi_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{i t^{\!\top}X}]$, which always exists
($|e^{i\theta}|=1$) and obeys the same theorem. For the Gaussian the MGF exists
everywhere, so we use the simpler object.
:::

## The MGF of a Gaussian — scalar case

$X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$. Everything lives in the exponent:

$$M_X(t) = \int e^{tx}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\,e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}\,dx$$

::: {.fragment}
**Complete the square** in the exponent:

$$tx - \frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}
= \underbrace{\mu t + \tfrac12\sigma^2 t^2}_{\text{free of } x}
\;-\; \frac{(x - \mu - \sigma^2 t)^2}{2\sigma^2}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
The first part leaves the integral; the rest is a Gaussian density with mean
$\mu + \sigma^2 t$, which integrates to $1$:

$$\boxed{\;M_X(t) = \exp\!\big(\mu t + \tfrac12 \sigma^2 t^2\big)\;}$$
:::

## …and in $d$ dimensions

For $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$ the coordinates are independent, so the
expectation factorises:

$$M_Z(t) = \prod_i \mathbb{E}\big[e^{t_i Z_i}\big] = \prod_i e^{t_i^2/2} = e^{\frac12 t^{\!\top}t}$$

::: {.fragment}
For $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)$, substitute $x = \mu + Lu$ with
$\Sigma = LL^{\!\top}$. The Jacobian $\det L$ cancels the $(\det\Sigma)^{1/2}$ in
the constant, leaving the standard case at $L^{\!\top}t$:

$$\boxed{\;M_X(t) = \exp\!\Big(t^{\!\top}\mu + \tfrac12\, t^{\!\top}\Sigma\, t\Big)\;}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Remember the shape: the exponent is a quadratic in $t$.** Everything below
follows from that alone. (This was a change of variables in an integral, not the
affine theorem — so no circularity.)
:::

## Step 2 — compute the MGF of $Y = AX + b$

$$M_Y(t) = \mathbb{E}\big[e^{t^{\!\top}Y}\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[e^{t^{\!\top}(AX+b)}\big]$$

[definition of the MGF, then substitute $Y = AX+b$]{.step}

::: {.fragment}
$$= e^{t^{\!\top}b}\;\mathbb{E}\big[e^{t^{\!\top}AX}\big]$$

[$b$ is constant, so $e^{t^{\!\top}b}$ leaves the expectation]{.step}
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$= e^{t^{\!\top}b}\;\mathbb{E}\big[e^{(A^{\!\top}t)^{\!\top}X}\big]$$

[since $t^{\!\top}A = (A^{\!\top}t)^{\!\top}$]{.step}
:::

::: {.fragment}
**That third line is the move.** The matrix has been pushed off the random vector
and onto the *argument*. The expectation is now just $M_X$ evaluated at the point
$A^{\!\top}t$ — and we know $M_X$.
:::

## Step 2 — recognise what comes out

Apply the Gaussian MGF at $A^{\!\top}t$:

$$M_Y(t) = e^{t^{\!\top}b}\exp\!\Big((A^{\!\top}t)^{\!\top}\mu + \tfrac12 (A^{\!\top}t)^{\!\top}\Sigma (A^{\!\top}t)\Big)$$

::: {.fragment}
$$= \exp\!\Big(t^{\!\top}b + t^{\!\top}\!A\mu + \tfrac12\, t^{\!\top}\!A\Sigma A^{\!\top}t\Big)$$

[transpose each piece]{.step}
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$= \exp\!\Big(t^{\!\top}\big(A\mu + b\big) + \tfrac12\, t^{\!\top}\big(A\Sigma A^{\!\top}\big)t\Big)$$

[collect the linear terms]{.step}
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Now read it.** The result has the form $\exp\big(t^{\!\top}m + \tfrac12 t^{\!\top}S t\big)$
— linear plus quadratic, exactly a Gaussian MGF, with $m = A\mu+b$ and
$S = A\Sigma A^{\!\top}$. By uniqueness, $Y$ *is* that Gaussian. $\blacksquare$
:::

## What actually did the work

- The Gaussian MGF has a **quadratic exponent**, and $A^{\!\top}t$ substituted
  into a quadratic is still a quadratic. That is the whole mechanism
- Push almost any other family through a linear map and the functional form
  changes — you leave the family and lose the closed form
- Equivalently, by change of variables: $y = Ax+b$ has $x = A^{-1}(y-b)$ and a
  *constant* Jacobian $|\det A|^{-1}$, so a quadratic exponent stays quadratic.
  The MGF route is shorter and does not need $A$ invertible

::: {.note}
This closure is the entire reason diffusion models are analytically tractable:
$p(x_t \mid x_0)$ has a closed form at every $t$ because every step is affine.
:::

## Read it in both directions

Factor $\Sigma = LL^{\!\top}$ (Cholesky, or $\Sigma^{1/2}$).

**Forward — sampling.** Take $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and set $A = L$, $b = \mu$:

$$\mu + Lz \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\big(\mu,\ L I L^{\!\top}\big) = \mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)$$

**Backward — whitening.** Take $A = L^{-1}$, $b = -L^{-1}\mu$:

$$L^{-1}(X - \mu) \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\big(0,\ L^{-1}\Sigma L^{-\top}\big) = \mathcal{N}(0,I)$$

::: {.note}
One theorem, applied twice. This is why you may always assume $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$
without loss of generality — and how a sampler turns standard noise into any
Gaussian you like.
:::

## The degenerate case

If $\operatorname{rank}(A) < d$, then $A\Sigma A^{\!\top}$ is **singular**:
$\det = 0$, and the density formula breaks down.

$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \det\big(A\Sigma A^{\!\top}\big) = 0$$

- The law is still Gaussian, but it lives on a **lower-dimensional subspace**
- It has no density with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^m$
- The theorem survives; only the *density formula* fails

::: {.note}
This is the same singularity as the manifold hypothesis, reached deliberately
rather than by accident. Real image data is believed to sit on exactly such a
thin set.
:::

## Where this lands

| Today | Where it returns |
|---|---|
| $AX+b$ closure | $p(x_t \mid x_0)$ in closed form at every noise level |
| $\mu + Lz$ | how every Gaussian sample is drawn, from standard noise |
| Whitening | why $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ costs no generality |
| Independent sum | variances add — the $\sqrt{t}$ envelope of the forward process |
| Singular $A\Sigma A^{\!\top}$ | data on a manifold; why densities are the wrong object there |

## {.accent}

::: {.quote}
Affine maps move a Gaussian's mean and reshape its covariance — but never take
it out of the family.
